Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as 'biggest breakthrough in decades'

Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as 'biggest breakthrough in decades'

AI 作者 rafaelc 热度 1393 回复 331 2026/11/21 05:03
打开原帖 打开外部链接 JSON

摘要

  • A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades.In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib, during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.Though doctors have said the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission.Half of all people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, and only about 3% of patients survive for five years when the disease spreads to other organs. It has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK and has a similarly poor prognosis globally.Patients were followed for a year and a half during the trial on average and some did not see the cancer return during this period. Longer studies will be conducted to see if any of the cancers can be put into remission. During the trial, tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients, just over 60% of patients had their tumours shrink or disappear, and for about 8% of patients tumours became undetectable on CT scans.A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year.Dr Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, who presented the findings, said “this is the closest to cure”, adding that he had never seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread.He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. “We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival,” he said.“The median follow-up is 18 months. Just imagine, in an average of 18 months your disease just disappears on the CT scan … that’s closest to complete remission … it’s incredible.”Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment, which works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations found in most pancreatic cancers. These mutations drive tumour growth.There are hopes the treatment could work for dozens of other cancers because they can have similar mutations.Michelle Mitchell, Cancer Research UK’s chief executive, said more research was needed, but added: “This is the biggest leap forward we’ve seen in decades for pancreatic cancer patients and could offer real hope to people facing one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat cancers.“These results raise the exciting possibility that this breakthrough could eventually pave the way for treating other cancers that carry Kras gene mutations. More trials are now needed before this treatment can be assessed for use on the NHS and despite this advance, pancreatic cancer survival is still very low.”

nik_s 2026/11/22 05:41
I think the layman's perception of the increase in survival (~13 months versus ~6 months) will make this look underwhelming. Nevertheless, it's important to remember that the incentives for clinical trials is to only include very late-stage patients who have exhausted all other options (faster trials, smaller sample sizes, surrogate endpoints, a shot at accelerated approval, ...). The fact that a treatment shows promise for these patients that are often in very poor health and considered "hopeless" by today's medicine is exceedingly rare, and the signal from this trial is indeed strong.

The (somewhat reasonable) hope is that patients 1. with earlier forms of pancreatic cancer (non-metastatic) 2. that can undergo surgery 3. together with a (neo)adjuvant treatment with these kras inhibitors, will end up having a much lower recurrence rate and a chance for a long, healthy life.

I think this is genuinely good news worth celebrating!

boplicity 2026/11/23 01:30
This is how most the world operates: people work hard to feed their families and provide security for them. It can be stressful. Money, of course, isn't earned for the sake of money, at least not for most people. That's the claim in the original quote that is completely wrong. Rather, we need money in order to buy food and all of the things that make life decent.

Also, what the quote gets totally wrong: Wealth is strongly correlated with good health. People generally earn more money and become more healthy. Not the other way around, in general, at least.

This is also how the world works: You're quietly eating on a field, when suddenly, you're a meal for an eagle, or a coyote, or a fox. It's short, painful, and brutal. Far better to deal with money, in my opinion, than the harsh reality of the natural world.

The thing with Buddhism is the notion that many of our injuries are self inflicted or even conjured out of nowhere, and you just exhibited a top shelf example of that.

What I quoted has absolutely nothing to do with karma, and everything to do with how scared you are of dying with regrets. I understand the people who want to see their kid graduate. But just in general principle? Fighting for two more months when even more of that time will be in agony than if you did nothing, and spending your kids inheritance to do that? Why do we do that to ourselves? And why do we sign them up to watch? You can sort out your conflicts with your friends and family in a week, or you can’t sort them out at all. Car wrecks and heart attacks take even that away. At least a terminal illness gives you a last call.

Cancer is cruel. Cancer treatment is only less cruel, and still cruel enough that people volunteer to work in cancer wards to make the patients a little more comfortable (my ex signed up for one but couldn’t follow through).

“Time” is not a reason to stay. It’s a placeholder for magic thinking or something you don’t want to face. And when someone asks YOU what you want to have before you die, you’d better have an answer or you’ll waste it. “Time” is the answer you give when you don’t know the answer and you’re hoping you’ll think of it later. By the time you’re fifty you’ll already know that’s bullshit, or you’ll be buried having never suspected.
